title: The food that ran away
hookLine: the self makes food, and the food turns and runs
carry: no single power is the self
tomorrow: the text asks one question twice. why won't the first answer do?

cards: One in the morning, and the phone is playing cooking videos. Butter hissing in a pan. Someone tearing open warm bread.
A whole video of it, and the stomach is exactly as empty as before. The Aitareya Upanishad tells a story about that very problem. The self has just made a person and moved the powers in.
Then it makes food. And the food, the text says, turns around and runs.

teach.h: SPEECH, BREATH, EYE, EAR: ALL MISS.
teach.b: So the chase begins. First the self tries to catch the food with speech, and can't. The text adds a line that's funny on purpose: if speech had caught it, a person would be full just from saying the word food.
Next, breath. If breath had caught it, smelling food would be enough. Then the eye: seeing food would fill you.
The ear: hearing about food would do it. Touch.
Then the mind: just thinking about a meal would be a meal. One by one, every power the person has reaches out, and the food slips away.
At last the self tries apana, the breath that draws in and down, the one that takes food in. That one catches it. Why tell a story about lunch in a book well-known for one of the great sayings?
Each power is real, and each does its own job well. The eye really sees. The mind really pictures.

teach.h: NO ONE POWER IS THE WHOLE PERSON.
teach.b: But not one of them, alone, is the whole person, and not one of them, alone, is satisfied.
The chase clears the table for the question this week keeps asking: if every power is only one part, what knows all of them at once?
This is one of the big teachings of the Upanishads, named plainly: you are not your eyes, your hunger or even your mind. The self, the atman, is the knowing they all report to.
And the Aitareya's answer goes further: prajnanam brahma, the knowing is Brahman.

how: Students of the Aitareya Upanishad read its opening stories, the powers entering the person and the chase after food, with a teacher as the setting for the great saying prajnanam brahma.

o: four great sayings that name the self as Brahman
four prayers said before a meal in the Vedas
four rules for the four stages of a life

games.q: the chase after the food. tap the pairs.
p: would fill you just by saying food
would fill you just by seeing food
would fill you just by thinking of food
the breath that finally catches it

s: the Upanishads treat the body and its senses as unimportant
in this story every power is real and does its job. none of them alone is the whole person.
in the Aitareya's story, the food runs away from the self
it turns and flees; speech, breath, eye, ear, touch and mind all fail to catch it.
the text says thinking about food can fill you
it jokes the other way: if the mind had caught the food, thinking would be a meal. it didn't.

games.q: a friend says: 'i read about meditation all week, so i'm basically calm now.' by the food story, what's the honest reply?
o: reading about it is like seeing food: real, but it doesn't fill you.
right: once the mind grasps an idea, the work is done.
reading is useless; only the body ever counts.
games.why: in the Aitareya, the eye and the mind each reach for the food and stay hungry. one power alone, even a sharp mind, isn't the whole of it.

practice: If there's something to eat nearby, a raisin, a cracker, a sip of tea, first just look at it. Then smell it. Then taste it, slowly.
At each step, notice which power is reaching out, and notice the quiet knowing that's aware of every one of them.

wordCard.voice: The four mahavakyas: the great sayings. This week's is prajnanam brahma, and today's story sets the table for it. Every power reaches; something knows the reaching.

orig.note: Sanskrit annam, food: what the self makes for the person, and what runs away in the Aitareya's story.

carryVoice: Your line: no single power is the self. Every one reaches; something knows the reaching. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Aitareya Upanishad 1.3.1–10 (the self creates food; the food turns and flees; the self tries to seize it with speech, breath, eye, ear, skin, mind and the rest, and fails, the text adding that otherwise one would be satisfied merely by speaking of, smelling, seeing, hearing, touching or thinking of food; it seizes it with apana)
